I remember a while ago some had suggested that a way to kill off open models in the US was to persuade govt/Congress to pass a safety-based set of rules/laws. For example, in order to be used by the federal govt and its vendors, an AI model must pass certain safety requirements. 

Such safety requirements will likely be formulated, with input about best practices from the leading US AI labs who likely could easily clear them. However, they could be costly, onerous if not outright impossible for smaller AI labs or foreign AI models to satisfy. So safety becomes eventually the reason they drop out of the US market. 

I’m not sure why but recent discussions about safety increasingly remind me of this idea.

Your RWA coins may have sold off, but there’s still plenty of interesting opportunities 

Here are three I’m watching today:

1. B-money (BSC)

@bmoneyonbnb is a BSC reflection token at $8m market cap. It charges 1% on buys and sells, converts the fee into BTCB and distributes it to qualifying self-custodied holders; more than 2 BTCB has reportedly been distributed

Think: 

b-money / wrapped BTC
@weidai11 Cypherpunk ’98 / Satoshi ’08

Currently volume implies approximately $23K in daily BTCB at a 1% tax. At a steadier $300K daily volume, annual distributions would be around $1.1m

Rewards depend on trading volume, while holders retain token-price and BTCB custody risk

2. Standard Reserve (RH)

@standard_rsv is scheduled to launch today on Robinhood Chain

STANDARD has a 1B hard cap. The first 100M tokens fund permanent protocol-owned Uniswap v4 liquidity. The remaining 900M form an issuance budget, with tokens minted when banker balances are withdrawn

Net ETH flow through the official pool determines policy:

i) Positive flow raises issuance and routes 70% of protocol ETH towards reserve assets such as tokenized gold
ii) Negative or zero flow cuts issuance and sends that 70% towards buybacks and burns. Another 15% adds permanent liquidity; 15% goes to the team

Its 1,000 Charter NFTs (0.15 ETH mint) are participation licences. Opening Branches burns STANDARD; withdrawals retire Branches and charge a variable fee split between burns and remaining bankers

My initial scenario is a:

1) $10M - $30M market cap if Charter demand, liquidity + reserve accumulation persist
2) > $50M would require material reserves, consistent fee flow and burns capable of offsetting withdrawals

Key risks are contract complexity, latent supply in unwithdrawn balances and reliance on one pool as the policy signal; there’s a lot of hype currently so my focus is medium to long term PA as @0xbeans is a genuine actor + long term aligned

3. LOTTO ( @Base)

Trading fees fund $1 @megapot tickets. Purchases return a 10% self-referral rebate to a restricted burn reserve. Winnings enter the same reserve, which buys LOTTO through a rising-price auction and burns the tokens. Mechanics⁠

It has already won a $213K jackpot… next megapot in 8 hours

A batch tickets purchased on Sept 12th contained the winning numbers for the September 13 draw. The $213k jackpot was paid to Lotto Coin one minute after drawing, with the purchase, draw and claim verifiable on Base

Under LOTTO’s design, that capital funds buybacks and burns rather than holder distributions

Against its $2.6M snapshot valuation, the jackpot equals 8.2% of market cap. It will not automatically burn 8.2% of supply; the auction clearing price and seller participation determine the final amount

Megapot’s founder said traffic and ticket purchases crashed its backend, temporarily hiding LOTTO’s transactions in the app

The current draw and its displayed estimates are separate from this win

Using Megapot’s 77.5% long-run prize return plus LOTTO’s 10% rebate, every $10K spent on tickets implies roughly $8,750 expected to reach the burn reserve across many draws. Individual results remain variable + could be interesting on token PA when large Megapots are up for grabs 

The strategic angle is Megapot. If it becomes the default onchain lottery rail, LOTTO could retain first-mover exposure as its flagship autonomous buyer and case study

That is narrative exposure, not a claim on Megapot revenue. A disclosed, vested Megapot stake in LOTTO could align incentives and add credibility. It could also create a conflict if Megapot favoured a token whose fees buy its tickets. Genuine economic exposure would require revenue sharing or reciprocal ownership, not simply Megapot holding LOTTO

There’ve been plenty of other projects creating tangible value across these ecosystems. I’ll provide more insights in tomorrow’s edition of my free newsletter. Link in bio

Let me know if any other novel projects below👇

The experiment ↓

When @Plasma (crypto card) was just launching, they were invite-only, and I had unlimited invite codes to share (unlike other users, who had just 3).

During that time, at @GREEND0TS we were onboarding several clients within the same vertical, so I decided to run a quick $500 test to see how non-Web3 users convert.

My thesis was to target CIS expats in Europe (Telegram communities), while others were targeting LatAm.

Two factors:

• Most of these people are well familiar with crypto transfers
• They have residence in permitted countries
• They are quite young, so likely less conservative

So I contacted a few relevant channels – and since Plasma gave me data on my code usage, I have conversion data to share:

- Total spend: $445
- Total reach: 35,000 views
- CPM: $12.7 (much lower vs. avg. Web3 reach)
- New signups: 18 ($24 cost per signup)
- Completed KYC: 4 ($111 per KYC)

Overall, this is within scalable acquisition benchmarks. I have clients with similar products who are ok paying $60–$80 per KYC, and with better ad text or targeting, this experiment could be viable.

Unfortunately, I had no data on their spend. Since I have almost 200 referrals on Plasma, I can only roughly estimate their total volume, but I can’t isolate the experiment with the CIS guys.

It’s unlikely, though, that the referral fees exceeded my ad investment, haha – however, this was not the goal.
Now, why I'm saying that the signals are very mixed.

1. View-to-signup ratio is very low.

2. Admins I bought ads from said they received a lot of skepticism and criticism about this placement, because for normies anything crypto-related can look like a scam.

3. Plasma is a well-known brand for Web3 people, but a no-name for normies. So they were reluctant to convert, especially in communities with group chats (people started a panic wave).

4. That’s why, even if they downloaded the app, they didn’t complete KYC, which was the final onboarding step.

Lessons learned:

• For Web3 products: If you’re expanding into non-crypto communities, run an awareness campaign first. For example, if you plan to target people in Berlin, I’d even consider buying banners there (yes, on the streets) before you start targeting local communities. This will likely improve CR dramatically.

• For all types of products: Buying ads where your competitors aren’t buying can be very promising. You might miss with a few categories, but overall the ROI is worth testing, imo.

• Regarding the channel: Telegram can deliver very good CPM and potentially strong conversions, but you need to know how to separate fake engagement from real engagement (this is a huge problem; if you’re interested, I can share some data).

Everyone knows about pons.

Here are 6 underrated dApps on Robinhood you should pay attention to:

1. @PareStocks ($PARE): A Pendle-style model for stocks.

Pare splits a tokenized stock into two tokens. PT is the stock at a discount, no dividends. YT is every dividend it earns. Merge them back any time, free.

Protocol revenue goes to deepening those markets and buying back and burning PARE. The team flags that early pools are thin, and the market cap only crossed $1M two weeks ago.

Most experimental one on this list, and the one I'm least sure about. The mechanism is clever. What I haven't seen is demand for trading those separate exposures. Demand for the PARE ticker is a different thing.

2. @sherwoodagent ($WOOD): AI-managed investment funds.

Sherwood is building onchain funds where agents propose strategies, depositors can vote them down, and guardians check every transaction before it executes.

WOOD is what guardians stake to do that job. Correct calls earn fees (capped at 5% guardian fee). Approving malicious calldata gets you slashed. No emissions, no mint after TGE.

It's a ~$5.6M market cap, ~82% off its high, and the docs still describe testnet. Mainnet is the milestone. I'm not calling this adoption yet.

3. @fablesfi ($PROLOGUE): The pre-launch DEX play.

Fables is a ve(3,3) DEX on Uniswap v4 with fees tailored to the asset. Stock market hours for tokenized equities, volatility for crypto. It's live: $10M+ in deposits and ~$200M volume in week two.

PROLOGUE converts to FABLES at TGE, reportedly 40:1 (1B PROLOGUE → 25M FABLES). It's trading around a $17M market cap.

That conversion is the whole trade. Work out what 25M FABLES is worth at a realistic launch FDV, then decide if $17M is cheap. PROLOGUE's own chart tells you nothing.

4. @NetNetCap ($NET): The treasury play.

A reserve-backed token in the OlympusDAO v1 lineage, rebuilt without a policy committee. USDG treasury, bond sales, buybacks, all formulaic. It reports backing per token, so you can compare it to market price directly.

Two things to know. There's a 5% fee on mapped AMM pairs (v4 and UniswapX dodge it, permanently). And staking pays zero at or below backing, full rate only at a 1.75x premium. Its tokenized stock holdings sit outside the reserves that count toward backing.

~$66M FDV, and it's already round tripped from ~$1,970 to ~$990. The question is whether backing can grow faster than the market prices in. "Reserve-backed" doesn't make something cheap.

5. @TheIndexFi ($INDEX): Trading fees turned into stock payouts.

Every INDEX trade takes a 3% fee in ETH, buys a basket of 18 tokenized stocks, and drops them into holders' wallets every 15 minutes. No staking, no claiming. Its Indices product routes fees the same way plus locked liquidity for INDEX.

The numbers are small. ~$456K in fees over 30 days, ~$291K to holders (per DefiLlama), against a market cap in the $30M+ range. So the yield is real but it's not the reason to own it.

The bet is that the fee-to-stock mechanic pulls more volume. Judge the payouts against what you paid for INDEX, and whether the trading funding them lasts.

6. @shroom_network ($SHROOM): Stock-token liquidity with a burn mechanism.

SHROOM owns 48 pools (and counting) pairing itself against stock tokens like NVDA, MSFT, and MU. It earns fees on all of it, including the price gaps between the token and the real stock when markets are closed.

V2 changed the flywheel. Stock token fees route back into their pools for depth. SHROOM fees now get burned, 13.6M so far.

~$16M market cap, down from a $40M+ high right after launch. I want to see recurring burns from real pool volume, not a burst around the announcement.

7. @ponsdotfamily ($PONS): The buyback play.

Gonna talk about Pons here since they're the biggest thing on Robinhood and going through a dip now.

~$108M in fees over the last 30 days, ~$20M of that protocol revenue (per DefiLlama). Peak day was $5.95M, more than Pump fun did that day.

80% of protocol revenue buys back and burns PONS. That's the protocol's 30% cut of the 1% trade fee, not 80% of everything traders pay. ~29% of supply is already gone. Market cap sits around $420M, down ~38% from the Sept 5 top.

Still my fav of the seven. It's exposure to launchpad activity without picking the next memecoin.

These are research leads, not recs to buy.

Anything on Robinhoodyou're bullish on that isn't here? Lemme know, gonna make a v2 in a few weeks.

• Ledger is staring down a $500M class action over its 2023 data breaches. The lead plaintiff lost nearly $2M to scammers pretending to be Ledger support.

• Harmony is shutting its mainnet after seven years and moving ONE to Ethereum. Deadline to exit smart contracts was Sept 10.

• Router Protocol is calling it after four years. Burning 303M ROUTE and pulling off CEXs before the Sept 30 shutdown.

Seven years for Harmony and 4 for Router. Nothing in this space is too old to die.

The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

Want to talk about this part of the Big Short where Burry closed down his fund: 

"Making money is not like I thought it would be. This business kills the part of life that is essential. The part that has nothing to do with business. For the past two years, my insides have felt like they’re eating themselves. All the people I respected won’t talk to me anymore except through lawyers. People want an authority to tell them how to value things, but they choose this authority not based on facts or results. They choose it because it seems authoritative and familiar. "

As we enter into late stage capitalism it is more important than ever to always remember that money and living life are completely at odds with each other - that the parts of life worth living - being happy, sharing things with your friends, living life, are all, really the anti-thesis of what capitalism, money, and greed all stand for

Personally the most important thing to do, is to balance it. Tao Te Ching by Lao Tzu is a good read on the Middle Way, and all of life can be applied to the concept of the Middle. Too many people get caught up in one way - and it's easy to get caught up in money - and forget the joys of simple living. 

To live this kind of life, you can think of your allocation of time on a weighing scale. Working a finance job - you lean too much on one side. Social media exacebates the worst side as well. You need to do things to balance the other side - dinner with friends, walking in parks, doing nothing, etc.
